baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Reconstructs how New York’s divided capital-owning elites became a more coherent bourgeoisie through institutions, cultural practices and political conflict (The Monied Metropolis, 2001).
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Author’s introduction pp. 2–3 and 6–9 read. Shared wealth does not automatically explain common identity or political power; class formation is the historical problem. This contribution brings elite formation into urban/social history without claiming Beckert founded the field or that the complete book’s cases have been independently verified.
baseline_incident_edges.map_label: Urban institutions and bourgeois class formation

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Contributes “war capitalism” as an account of the violent trading, land and labour arrangements from which industrial capitalism developed (Empire of Cotton, 2014; author’s explanation, 2019).
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: The authorised excerpt remains the existing limited book witness; Beckert’s LSE answer on the term was freshly read. His historical claim about links among armed trade, dispossession, enslavement and state power is attributed, not accepted as a settled causal explanation of industrialisation. The existing Hilt and Burnard/Riello partial readings and the new_history_of_capitalism strand retain their criticisms. Baptist-specific productivity claims are not assigned to Beckert.
baseline_incident_edges.map_label: War capitalism: violence, land, labour and states

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Explains a global method that relates merchants, plantations and manufacturing across regions, treating capitalism as connected diversity rather than a single preordained path (GrowthPolicy interview, 2020).
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Beckert’s second answer was read: comparative regional sites and linked labour regimes support this account of his method. A first-person research strategy does not establish universal adoption, prove every regional empirical claim, or derive a new argument from the unread 2025 book. The field’s prior approaches, Benton addition and review boundary remain intact.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Faust questions whether the New History of Slavery’s Capitalism,including Beckert’s work,adequately explains slaveholders’ ideas and regional cultural differences.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own2023 address names Johnson’s River of Dark Dreams,Beckert’s Empire of Cotton and Edward Baptist’s The Half Has Never Been Told as three major statements before criticizing the shared framework’s concentration on material self-interest. Baptist and Jones-Rogers are separate,more individually detailed examples;their specific claims are not reassigned to this target. Faust concedes possible economic connections while asking whether worldviews remained distinct. Original monographs and other economic critics’ articles unread.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Frank's ReOrient (1998) as the polemical wing of the divergence debate: Asia central until 1800, a debate with Landes announced for December 1998 and an endorsement of Pomeranz (2001)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Notice announcing the Landes–Frank debate (Northeastern University, scheduled for 2 December 1998; read; written from Frank's side; whether the debate took place as announced is not independently confirmed): 'FRANK retorts that … Received social theory … is vitiated by the ingrained EUROCENTRISM of historiography'; Asia 'remained predominant in the world until at 1800'; 'LANDES retorts that Frank and his echoes are a magnet for fallacies and fantasies'. Frank's review of Pomeranz (JAS 2001; author's manuscript read): 'bar none, the biggest and most important contribution'; Pomeranz is 'the most important … member of what Jack Goldstone has called the new "California School"'. Mokyr (EH.Net 2012, read): 'The California School, most notably embodied in Kenneth Pomeranz's Great Divergence and Andre Gunder Frank's Re-Orient'. Vries (2013, pp. 15–16) quotes ReOrient (pp. 75, 259) and calls one passage 'a quite silly statement'. Burnard and Riello (2020, p. 228 n.): Beckert 'is heavily influenced by [world-systems theory's] axioms'. ReOrient itself is unread. Distinct from edge_1053 (Pomeranz → dependency).

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Capitalism and Slavery (1944) as the starting point of the slavery-and-capitalism component: four arguments taken up and modified by economic historians and by the new history of capitalism
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Readers, read: Burnard and Riello (JGH 2020, p. 227): 'Four of his arguments are critical to the NHC project: that slavery was central to the Industrial Revolution; that slave wealth was important to the history of eighteenth-century Britain; that the West Indian slave economy went into decline from 1783; and that West Indian slave-owners moved from being a progressive force within mercantilism to being a reactionary force within industrial capitalism'; 'His contemporary defenders, however, use Williams for historical perspectives he never considered' (p. 227); 'a movement among economic historians that accepts a modified version of the Williams thesis' (p. 233). Hilt (JEH 2017, p. 516): 'Like Eric Williams in Capitalism and Slavery (1944), Beckert argues …'; n. 6: Inikori (2002) is 'the strongest recent defense of the Williams hypothesis'. Regele (2023, p. 7): the new work draws on 'a long history of scholarship … most notably Eric Williams's Capitalism and Slavery'. Pomeranz (2000, p. 3 n. 2): 'the generally negative current mainstream verdicts on the arguments of Eric Williams (1944)'. Distinct from edge_155 (Williams → economic) and edge_406 (Williams → atlantic).
